These limitations do not invalidate the method, but they mean SROI should be presented with its assumptions, sensitivity analysis and narrative context, and used alongside other forms of evidence.

sections.heading: When SROI is the right tool
paragraphs: SROI is most useful when an organization needs to understand and communicate the full value of a program, particularly when that value is largely social and would otherwise go unrecognized. It is well suited to informing decisions about which programs to expand, redesign or stop, to supporting conversations with commissioners and funders, and to clarifying how value is distributed among different stakeholder groups. A forecast SROI can test the logic of a new program before launch.

It is less suitable when outcomes cannot be credibly evidenced, when the main purpose is to produce an impressive ratio for marketing, or when resources do not allow genuine stakeholder engagement. In those cases, a simpler outcomes framework or a theory of change with a focused set of indicators may provide more reliable insight at lower cost. Choosing the right tool is itself part of good impact management. Organizations sometimes begin with a simpler approach and progress to SROI once their data and stakeholder relationships are strong enough to support it.

sections.heading: How Datalidity approaches SROI
paragraphs: Datalidity conducts SROI and related social value analyses with an emphasis on rigor, stakeholder voice and decision usefulness. Following our Listen, Measure, Design, Deliver, Sustain methodology, we engage participants, staff, partners and funders to understand what changes for them, gather and analyze evidence, and apply conservative adjustments and sensitivity testing consistent with the social value principles. Where evidence is thin, we say so, and we recommend practical ways to strengthen data collection for future analyses. Our goal is a result that a skeptical board member or commissioner can examine and trust.

We present results with full transparency about assumptions and limits, and we help clients use the findings to design better programs, allocate resources and build ongoing measurement systems. For many organizations, the most valuable outcome of an SROI process is not the ratio but a clearer understanding of what matters to the people they serve, and a practical way to manage toward it. We often connect SROI findings to dashboards and governance routines so that the insights inform ongoing program decisions.

faqs.q: How is SROI calculated?
faqs.a: An SROI analysis identifies the outcomes experienced by stakeholders, assigns monetary values to those outcomes using financial proxies, and adjusts for deadweight, attribution, displacement and drop-off. The adjusted value is projected over a defined period and discounted to present value. That total is divided by the value of the inputs invested to produce a ratio. Sensitivity analysis then tests how robust the result is to changes in key assumptions.

faqs.q: What is the difference between SROI and cost-benefit analysis?
faqs.a: Both compare the value of outcomes with the cost of achieving them. Cost-benefit analysis is typically conducted from a government or societal perspective and often focuses on outcomes with established economic values. SROI places greater emphasis on stakeholder involvement in defining and valuing outcomes, includes softer outcomes such as wellbeing, and is guided by a specific set of social value principles designed to prevent over-claiming.

faqs.q: Can SROI ratios be compared between organizations?
faqs.a: Generally not directly. SROI ratios depend on scope, stakeholder groups, chosen proxies, time horizons and adjustment assumptions, which vary considerably between analyses. Two programs with similar ratios may have very different evidence quality. Comparisons are more meaningful within one organization over time, or between programs analyzed with consistent methods. The underlying evidence, stakeholder insight and sensitivity analysis are more informative than the headline ratio.

insights.title: Jobs to Be Done
insights.meta_title: Jobs to Be Done (JTBD): Framework, Examples, Interviews
insights.meta_description: Jobs to be done explained: the theory behind JTBD, the functional, emotional and social dimensions of a job, how to run JTBD interviews, and how to apply it.
insights.summary: A practical guide to the jobs to be done framework: why people hire products and services, how to uncover their real jobs, and how to turn insight into strategy.
insights.dek: Jobs to be done is a way of understanding demand by asking what progress a person is trying to make in a particular circumstance. It shifts attention from customer demographics and product features to the underlying need that drives choice.
key_takeaways: Jobs to be done holds that people hire products and services to make progress in specific circumstances.
Clayton Christensen popularized the theory, with contributions from practitioners such as Bob Moesta and Tony Ulwick.
Jobs have functional, emotional and social dimensions, and competition includes any solution that does the same job.
The framework applies to services, internal programs and employee offerings as well as consumer products.

sections.heading: What jobs to be done means
paragraphs: Jobs to be done is a theory of customer motivation and a set of methods for uncovering it. Its central claim is that people do not buy products or services for their own sake. They hire them to get a job done: to make progress in a particular circumstance. A commuter who buys a morning milkshake, in the well-known example Clayton Christensen used, is not expressing a preference for dairy. They are hiring something to make a long, dull drive more bearable and to stay full until lunch. Understanding that job explains the purchase better than the commuter's age, income or stated preferences.

Christensen, the Harvard Business School professor best known for the theory of disruptive innovation, developed and popularized jobs to be done as a way to explain why so many innovations fail. Practitioners including Bob Moesta, who worked with Christensen on early applications, and Tony Ulwick, who developed an outcome-driven approach to innovation, built rigorous methods around the idea. Although their versions differ in emphasis, all share the conviction that the job, not the customer or the product, should be the primary unit of analysis for strategy and innovation.

sections.heading: The dimensions of a job
paragraphs: A job is rarely only functional. Most jobs have three dimensions that together explain why people choose one solution over another. The functional dimension describes the practical task to be accomplished. The emotional dimension describes how people want to feel, or avoid feeling, while doing it. The social dimension describes how they want to be perceived by others. A small business owner hiring an accounting service wants accurate books, but also peace of mind and credibility with lenders and investors. A solution that addresses only the functional job may lose to one that addresses all three.

Jobs are also defined by circumstance. The same person may have very different jobs depending on time, place and situation. This is why demographic segmentation often fails to predict behavior: two people with identical profiles may be hiring for different jobs, while two very different people may share the same one. Defining the circumstance precisely, including what triggered the search for a solution, is often the most valuable part of jobs to be done research.
bullets: Functional: the practical task the person needs to accomplish.
Emotional: how the person wants to feel during and after.
Social: how the person wants to be seen by others.
Circumstance: the context and trigger that make the job urgent.

sections.heading: Rethinking competition and value
paragraphs: Jobs to be done changes how organizations think about competition. If the job is the unit of analysis, then competitors include any solution a person might hire to do that job, including workarounds, doing nothing, or products from entirely different categories. A bank's mobile app may compete not only with other banks but with spreadsheets, a relative's advice or the decision to postpone a financial task. Seeing competition this way often reveals threats and opportunities that category-based analysis misses entirely.

The framework also clarifies what value means. Features matter only insofar as they help people make progress on the job. Many products and services accumulate features that do little for the core job while neglecting the frustrations people actually experience. Jobs to be done research identifies the forces that push people toward a new solution, the forces that pull them, and the anxieties and habits that hold them back. Addressing these forces, especially the anxieties of switching, is frequently more effective than adding capability.

sections.heading: How to uncover jobs to be done
paragraphs: The most common method is the switch interview, an in-depth conversation with someone who has recently started using a solution or stopped using one. Rather than asking what people want, which tends to produce speculation, interviewers reconstruct the actual timeline of the decision: the first thought that something needed to change, the moments of passive and active searching, the options considered, the deciding event and the experience afterward. Concrete stories reveal the real job, the circumstances and the forces at play far better than surveys or focus groups can.

Interview findings are then synthesized into job statements and patterns. Some practitioners go further, quantifying desired outcomes through surveys that measure how important each outcome is and how well current solutions satisfy it. This outcome-driven approach helps prioritize where to innovate. Whatever the method, discipline matters: interviewers must avoid leading questions, focus on past behavior rather than hypothetical preferences, and keep asking what progress the person was trying to make in their particular situation.

sections.heading: Applying jobs to be done beyond products
paragraphs: Although jobs to be done emerged in product innovation, it is equally powerful for services, public programs and internal offerings. A workforce development program can ask what job a participant is hiring it for: a credential, a route to a specific employer, structure during a difficult period or a sense of momentum. A public agency can ask what residents are really trying to accomplish when they contact it. An HR function can ask what job a manager is hiring a performance process to do, which is often quite different from what the process was designed for.

Applied internally, the framework helps organizations redesign employee programs around real needs. Benefits, learning platforms, internal tools and policies all compete for employees' limited time and attention, and they are frequently abandoned in favor of workarounds. Understanding the jobs employees are trying to get done, and the circumstances in which they struggle, leads to services that people actually use and value, rather than programs that look comprehensive on paper but go largely unused in practice.

sections.heading: How Datalidity applies jobs to be done
paragraphs: Datalidity uses jobs to be done as part of our customer strategy, service design and employee experience work. Within our Listen, Measure, Design, Deliver, Sustain methodology, switch interviews and contextual research help us listen for the real progress customers, residents, participants and employees are seeking. We then measure the importance and satisfaction of key outcomes to identify where unmet needs are largest and where current offerings fall short. This pairing of stories and numbers keeps the work grounded.

Those insights inform the design of services, programs and strategies built around real jobs rather than assumed preferences. We help teams translate findings into clear priorities, prototype and test new approaches, and track whether people are making the progress they came for. For organizations whose growth or mission depends on serving people well, jobs to be done provides a disciplined, evidence-based way to understand what those people actually need and why they choose as they do.

faqs.q: Who created the jobs to be done framework?
faqs.a: Jobs to be done is most closely associated with Clayton Christensen of Harvard Business School, who popularized the theory in his writing on innovation. Practitioners including Bob Moesta, who collaborated with Christensen and developed the switch interview approach, and Tony Ulwick, who developed outcome-driven innovation, shaped the methods used today. The underlying idea also echoes earlier marketing thought, such as Theodore Levitt's observation that people want the hole, not the drill.

faqs.q: What is a jobs to be done interview?
faqs.a: A jobs to be done interview, often called a switch interview, is an in-depth conversation with someone who recently adopted or abandoned a product or service. The interviewer reconstructs the timeline of the decision, from the first trigger to the purchase and subsequent experience, focusing on concrete events rather than opinions. The goal is to uncover the circumstances, the progress the person sought, and the forces that encouraged or inhibited switching.

faqs.q: How is jobs to be done different from personas?
faqs.a: Personas describe types of people, often with demographic and attitudinal details. Jobs to be done describes the progress people are trying to make in specific circumstances, independent of who they are. The same person may have different jobs in different situations, and very different people may share a job. Many teams use both, grounding personas in research on jobs so that they reflect real motivations rather than assumed characteristics.

insights.title: Service Blueprinting
insights.meta_title: Service Blueprinting: What It Is and How to Create One
insights.meta_description: Service blueprinting explained: the layers of a service blueprint, how it differs from a journey map, how to build one, and how to use it to drive change.
insights.summary: How a service blueprint connects the customer experience to the people, processes and systems behind it, and how to build one that leads to operational change.
insights.dek: A service blueprint is a diagram that shows how a service is delivered, linking what customers experience to the frontstage and backstage actions, support processes and systems that make it happen. It is the bridge between experience and operations.
key_takeaways: Service blueprinting was introduced by Lynn Shostack as a way to design services as deliberately as products.
A blueprint layers customer actions over frontstage, backstage and support processes, separated by lines of interaction and visibility.
Unlike a journey map, a blueprint shows the internal operations that create or break the experience.
Blueprints are most valuable when built with frontline staff and used to prioritize operational change.

sections.heading: What a service blueprint is
paragraphs: A service blueprint is a visual map of a service that shows the relationships between the customer's experience and the organizational activities that support it. It describes, step by step, what the customer does, what employees do in direct contact with the customer, what happens behind the scenes, and which processes and systems enable each step. By placing all of these on a single timeline, a service blueprint reveals how the organization produces the experience, and where it fails to.

The method was introduced by Lynn Shostack, a banking executive, in articles published in the Harvard Business Review and marketing journals in the early 1980s. Shostack argued that services, though intangible, could be designed with the same precision as products if their processes were made visible. Researchers including Mary Jo Bitner and colleagues later refined the technique, and it has since become a core tool in service design, customer experience management and operations improvement across healthcare, financial services, hospitality, government and many other sectors.

sections.heading: The anatomy of a service blueprint
paragraphs: Most service blueprints share a common structure. Horizontal lanes represent different layers of the service, and columns represent the steps of the customer journey over time. Physical evidence, the tangible things customers see or touch such as a website, a form, a waiting room or a confirmation email, is usually shown across the top. Three lines separate the lanes and carry important meaning: the line of interaction marks direct contact between customer and organization; the line of visibility separates what customers can see from what they cannot; and the line of internal interaction separates frontline staff from the support functions that serve them.

Arrows show dependencies and handoffs between lanes. Many teams add further layers, such as time, emotional state, policies, data flows, pain points or metrics, depending on the decisions the blueprint is meant to inform. The key is that every customer step can be traced down through the organization to the people, processes and systems responsible for it. That traceability is what makes a blueprint actionable: when a customer step fails, the diagram shows which team, process or system needs to change, and which other parts of the service depend on it. It also exposes steps that no one clearly owns, which are frequently where the worst experiences occur.
bullets: Physical evidence: tangible touchpoints the customer encounters.
Customer actions: the steps the customer takes throughout the service.
Frontstage actions: employee or system actions visible to the customer.
Backstage actions: employee actions that are invisible to the customer.
Support processes: internal functions and systems enabling the service.

sections.heading: Service blueprint vs. journey map
paragraphs: Journey maps and service blueprints are related but serve different purposes. A journey map describes the experience from the customer's perspective: the steps they take, what they think and feel, and where they encounter friction. It is primarily a tool for empathy and for identifying where the experience falls short. A service blueprint starts where the journey map ends. It takes the customer's journey as its top layer and then documents the operational reality beneath it, showing which activities, handoffs and systems produce each moment.

In practice, the two are often used in sequence. Research informs a journey map that highlights the moments that matter most. A blueprint then explains why those moments go wrong and what would need to change to fix them. The journey map tells leaders what to care about; the blueprint tells them where to intervene. Organizations that stop at journey mapping often struggle to act, because the causes of poor experience lie in operations that the journey map does not show.

sections.heading: How to create a service blueprint
paragraphs: Creating a useful service blueprint begins with a clear scope: a specific service, a specific customer segment and a specific scenario, such as a new patient booking a first appointment or a small business applying for a loan. Trying to blueprint everything at once produces diagrams too large to use. Research comes next. The customer layer should reflect actual behavior gathered through interviews and observation, and the backstage layers should be built with the employees who do the work, because documented procedures often differ from reality.

Teams then map each layer step by step, mark the lines of interaction and visibility, and draw the dependencies between them. Once the current state is complete, they annotate it with evidence about pain points, delays, failure points and costs. From there, they develop a future-state blueprint showing how the service should work, which becomes the basis for an implementation plan with owners and metrics. Validating both versions with frontline staff and, where possible, customers keeps the blueprint honest and builds support for change.
bullets: Define the service, customer segment and scenario to blueprint.
Research the customer journey through interviews and observation.
Map frontstage, backstage and support activities with frontline staff.
Mark lines of interaction, visibility and internal interaction.
Annotate failure points, wait times, handoffs and costs.
Design a future-state blueprint and an implementation plan.

sections.heading: Using blueprints to drive operational change
paragraphs: A service blueprint is most valuable when it changes decisions. Because it connects experience to operations, it helps leaders prioritize investments where they will have the greatest effect on both customer outcomes and internal efficiency. It exposes handoffs between departments that create delay, policies that force customers to repeat information, and systems that require employees to work around them. These are often invisible to executives who see only aggregated metrics, and the blueprint makes them concrete enough to act upon.

Blueprints also improve employee experience. Frontline staff frequently absorb the consequences of backstage failures, managing frustrated customers and inventing workarounds. Making those failures visible validates their experience and gives them a role in designing solutions. Finally, a blueprint is a powerful communication tool for cross-functional alignment. When operations, technology, HR and customer teams look at the same map, they can agree on shared priorities and clarify who owns each part of the service.

sections.heading: How Datalidity uses service blueprinting
paragraphs: Datalidity uses service blueprinting to connect people, process and performance. Within our Listen, Measure, Design, Deliver, Sustain methodology, we begin with research among customers and frontline employees, measure the operational and experience indicators that matter, and build current-state blueprints with the teams who deliver the service. That combination of qualitative insight and quantitative evidence makes the blueprint a credible basis for decisions. It also ensures the people closest to the work see their knowledge reflected in the map, which strengthens their commitment to the changes that follow from it.

We then co-design future-state blueprints, define the role, process, policy and technology changes required, and support implementation through change management and capability building. Because blueprints show both customers and employees, they are central to our belief that serving people well inside an organization is how it serves people well outside it. The result is a service that is easier to use, easier to deliver and easier to improve over time.

faqs.q: Who invented the service blueprint?
faqs.a: Service blueprinting was introduced by Lynn Shostack, a banking executive who published influential articles on service design in the early 1980s, including in the Harvard Business Review. She argued that services could be designed systematically if their processes were made visible. Later researchers, notably Mary Jo Bitner and colleagues, refined the technique and its standard structure of customer, frontstage, backstage and support process layers.

faqs.q: What is the difference between a service blueprint and a process map?
faqs.a: A process map documents the sequence of internal activities, usually from the organization's perspective, often to improve efficiency. A service blueprint starts with the customer's experience and links it to frontstage interactions, backstage activities and support processes. Its lines of interaction and visibility explicitly show how internal operations affect what customers see and feel. Blueprints are therefore better suited to improving experience and efficiency together.

faqs.q: How detailed should a service blueprint be?
faqs.a: Detail should match the decisions the blueprint is meant to inform. A high-level blueprint across a whole service can help leaders see where to focus. A detailed blueprint of a single scenario is needed to redesign specific processes, roles and systems. Most teams start broad to identify priorities and then create detailed blueprints for the moments where experience and operations most need improvement.

insights.title: Human Capital as a Value Creation Lever in Private Equity
insights.meta_title: Human Capital in Private Equity: A Value Creation Lever
insights.meta_description: How human capital drives value creation in private equity: leadership, talent, culture and workforce analytics across diligence, the hold period and exit.
insights.summary: Why leadership, talent, culture and workforce practices have become central to private equity value creation, and how sponsors can manage human capital across the deal lifecycle.
insights.dek: Private equity value creation increasingly depends on operational improvement rather than financial engineering, and operations run on people. Treating human capital as a disciplined value creation lever, from diligence through exit, is now a mark of sophisticated sponsors.
key_takeaways: As financial engineering yields less, operational value creation has made leadership and talent central to private equity returns.
Human capital due diligence assesses leadership, culture, organization and workforce risks before a deal closes.
During the hold period, leadership alignment, incentives, organizational design and retention drive execution of the value creation plan.
Strong human capital evidence also supports exit readiness by demonstrating durable, transferable leadership and workforce capability.

sections.heading: Why human capital matters in private equity
paragraphs: For much of the history of buyouts, returns relied heavily on debt financing and multiple expansion. As competition for deals intensified and the cost of capital rose and fell unpredictably, sponsors placed greater emphasis on operational value creation: growing revenue, improving margins, professionalizing management and executing add-on acquisitions. Every one of these levers depends on people. A value creation plan is only as strong as the leadership team that executes it and the workforce that delivers it day to day.

Human capital in private equity therefore refers to the leadership, talent, organizational structure, culture and workforce practices of portfolio companies, considered as drivers of enterprise value. Leading sponsors increasingly treat these factors with the same rigor as financial and commercial diligence. Many have built operating partner teams with talent expertise, standardized leadership assessments across their portfolios, and introduced workforce metrics into board reporting. The underlying recognition is that leadership and talent problems are among the most frequent causes of underperformance, and among the most preventable.

sections.heading: Human capital due diligence
paragraphs: Value creation begins before a deal closes. Human capital due diligence assesses whether the target company has the leadership, organization and workforce needed to deliver the investment thesis. It examines the capabilities and gaps of the management team, key-person dependencies, organizational design, culture, compensation and incentive structures, workforce stability and engagement, and labor-related risks. It also considers how the culture of the target will interact with the sponsor's operating style or with a platform company in a buy-and-build strategy.

Good human capital diligence goes beyond reviewing organization charts and employment contracts. It combines structured leadership assessment, interviews, analysis of workforce data such as turnover, tenure and pay, and, where access allows, employee sentiment. Its findings should feed directly into deal valuation, the structure of management incentives and the first-hundred-day plan, so that identified gaps are addressed quickly rather than discovered later at greater cost. Diligence conducted this way also gives the incoming board an early, shared view of the leadership team's strengths and development needs.
bullets: Leadership capability against the specific demands of the investment thesis.
Key-person risks and the depth of succession behind critical roles.
Organizational design, spans, layers and decision rights.
Culture, engagement and the likely response to ownership change.
Pay competitiveness, incentive alignment and retention exposure.
Workforce compliance, labor relations and reputational risks.

sections.heading: Human capital during the hold period
paragraphs: Once the deal closes, human capital becomes a central execution lever. The first priority is usually leadership alignment: ensuring the management team shares the value creation plan, understands their roles in it, and has the capability to deliver. This may involve leadership assessment, executive coaching, targeted hiring or restructuring the top team. Incentive design, typically including management equity, must align leaders with the plan while being perceived as fair by the broader organization.

Beyond the top team, organizational design and workforce planning ensure the company has the right structure and skills for its next phase. Retention of critical talent, especially during periods of change such as integrations or carve-outs, protects institutional knowledge and customer relationships. Culture and employee experience affect productivity, quality and the company's ability to recruit. Sponsors that track a small set of leading people indicators, such as regretted turnover, internal fill rates and engagement in critical roles, can spot execution risks early and intervene before they affect financial results.

sections.heading: Human capital and exit readiness
paragraphs: At exit, buyers assess whether the company's performance can continue under new ownership. A strong, stable leadership team with clear succession, a professionalized organization, documented talent processes and healthy workforce metrics all reduce perceived risk. Conversely, heavy dependence on a founder or a few executives, high turnover in critical roles or cultural instability can depress valuation or complicate the transaction. Buyers increasingly probe these issues directly in their own diligence, interviewing leaders and examining workforce data, so weaknesses that were tolerated during the hold period can become negotiating points at exactly the wrong moment.

Preparing human capital for exit should begin well before a sale process. Sponsors can strengthen succession plans, deepen the leadership bench, resolve organizational issues and assemble evidence of people practices and outcomes. Increasingly, buyers and limited partners also look at workforce-related ESG factors, including job quality, health and safety, and pay equity, which makes credible human capital data part of the equity story. A company that can demonstrate a durable, capable organization is easier to sell and easier to underwrite.

sections.heading: Building a portfolio-level human capital capability
paragraphs: Sponsors that consistently create value through human capital tend to build repeatable capabilities at the fund level. These include standardized leadership assessment frameworks, playbooks for the first hundred days, talent networks for rapid executive hiring, common people metrics in board reporting and shared approaches to incentive design. A portfolio-level view also enables comparison across companies, revealing patterns in leadership effectiveness and workforce health that individual boards might miss. It also helps sponsors deploy scarce operating resources where they will have the most effect, rather than spreading attention evenly across companies with very different needs.

This capability does not require a large in-house team, but it does require clear ownership and consistent methods. Many firms combine a small internal talent function with specialist external support for diligence, assessment and transformation work. The aim is to make human capital as visible and manageable as financial performance, so that people risks and opportunities are addressed systematically rather than reactively, and so that each new investment benefits from lessons learned across the portfolio.

sections.heading: How Datalidity supports private equity sponsors
paragraphs: Datalidity advises private equity sponsors and portfolio companies on the people side of value creation. Through our Listen, Measure, Design, Deliver, Sustain methodology, we listen to leaders and employees, measure leadership capability, culture and workforce health with rigorous data, and design organizational, leadership and incentive solutions aligned with the investment thesis. We support delivery through integration, change management and coaching, and we build the dashboards and governance routines that let boards track people indicators alongside financial ones. Our emphasis is on practical, evidence-based judgments that deal teams and operating partners can act on within the timelines that transactions demand.

We work across the deal lifecycle, from human capital due diligence and value creation planning to portfolio leadership assessment, post-merger integration and exit readiness. Our impact orientation means we also help sponsors understand how workforce practices affect communities and stakeholders, which matters to limited partners and buyers alike. The goal is to make human capital a measurable, managed driver of durable value, not an afterthought discovered when performance falters. Sponsors gain clearer insight into risk, faster execution and a stronger story at exit.

faqs.q: What is human capital due diligence in private equity?
faqs.a: Human capital due diligence is the assessment of a target company's leadership, organization, culture and workforce before an investment. It evaluates management capability against the investment thesis, key-person and succession risks, organizational design, compensation and incentives, workforce stability and engagement, and labor-related risks. Its findings inform valuation, management incentive design and the post-close plan, helping sponsors address people risks early rather than after they affect performance.

faqs.q: How do private equity firms create value through human capital?
faqs.a: Sponsors create value through human capital by ensuring the right leadership team is in place, aligning incentives with the value creation plan, designing an organization fit for growth, retaining critical talent, and improving culture and workforce productivity. Many also standardize leadership assessment and people metrics across their portfolios. These efforts support faster execution of operational improvements and strengthen the company's position at exit.

faqs.q: When should human capital be considered in a deal?
faqs.a: Human capital should be considered from the earliest stages of evaluating a deal and throughout the investment. It informs diligence and valuation before closing, shapes the first hundred days and value creation plan after closing, guides leadership and organizational decisions during the hold period, and supports exit readiness. Sponsors who address human capital only when problems emerge typically face higher costs and slower execution.

insights.title: Change Fatigue and How to Prevent It
insights.meta_title: Change Fatigue: Causes, Warning Signs and How to Prevent It
insights.meta_description: Change fatigue explained: what causes it, the warning signs leaders should watch for, and practical ways to prevent it with prioritization, design and support.
insights.summary: What causes change fatigue, how to recognize it before it undermines execution, and how leaders can sequence, design and support change so people can absorb it.
insights.dek: Change fatigue is the exhaustion, cynicism and disengagement that build when people face too much change, poorly managed, for too long. It is one of the most common reasons good strategies stall, and it is largely preventable.
key_takeaways: Change fatigue arises from the cumulative load of change, not any single initiative, and is often invisible to senior leaders.
Warning signs include declining participation, rising cynicism, slower adoption and increased turnover in affected teams.
Prevention starts with portfolio-level prioritization and sequencing, so the total load matches people's capacity to absorb it.
Involving people in designing change, and supporting managers, builds resilience and makes change feel done with them, not to them.

sections.heading: What change fatigue is
paragraphs: Change fatigue is a state of exhaustion, resignation and reduced commitment that develops when employees experience a high volume of organizational change over a sustained period, especially change that feels poorly explained, inadequately supported or disconnected from visible results. It shows up as apathy toward new initiatives, skepticism about leadership intentions, and a tendency to wait for the latest program to pass. It differs from resistance to change. Resistance is often active and focused on a specific change; fatigue is passive and cumulative.

Change fatigue matters because modern organizations are rarely implementing only one change at a time. Technology upgrades, restructurings, new processes, acquisitions, policy shifts and cultural initiatives often run in parallel, each sponsored by a different leader who sees only their own project. For employees, particularly in frontline and middle management roles, these initiatives arrive together and compete for the same limited time, attention and emotional energy. The result can be a workforce that is willing in principle but unable in practice to absorb more.

sections.heading: What causes change fatigue
paragraphs: The primary cause is cumulative load. Each initiative may be reasonable on its own, but leaders rarely see the total burden landing on particular teams. A second cause is poor change management: unclear rationale, inconsistent communication, inadequate training and insufficient time to learn new ways of working. A third is a history of initiatives that were launched with fanfare and then abandoned, which teaches employees that waiting is a rational response. Each failed initiative makes the next one harder.

Other factors amplify fatigue. When people have no voice in how change is designed, they feel it is being done to them. When managers are themselves overloaded or unconvinced, they cannot support their teams. When change coincides with heavy workloads, staffing shortages or job insecurity, the emotional cost rises sharply. Research on organizational change consistently points to the importance of perceived fairness, participation and support in determining how people respond to change.
bullets: Too many concurrent initiatives landing on the same teams.
Unclear purpose or inconsistent messages about why change is needed.
A track record of abandoned or unfinished initiatives.
Little employee voice in how changes are designed.
Overloaded managers without the time or tools to support teams.
Insufficient training, resources or time to adopt new ways of working.

sections.heading: Warning signs leaders should watch
paragraphs: Change fatigue is often invisible to senior leaders, because people tend to signal compliance upward while expressing frustration among peers. Leaders should therefore look for indirect signals. Participation in feedback channels and change activities may decline. Adoption of new systems or processes may stall at partial levels, with workarounds persisting. Cynical humor about new initiatives may become common. Absence, turnover and requests for transfers may rise in heavily affected teams, and engagement survey comments may refer to initiative overload or a lack of follow-through.

Quantitative indicators help, but listening is essential. Pulse surveys focused on change load and capacity, short interviews with managers and frontline staff, and analysis of which teams are affected by which initiatives can together build a realistic picture. The goal is to detect rising fatigue early, while there is still time to adjust the pace or sequence of change, rather than after key initiatives have already stalled or key people have left.

sections.heading: How to prevent change fatigue
paragraphs: Prevention starts at the portfolio level. Leaders should maintain a single view of all significant initiatives, the teams each will affect and when, and the capacity those teams have to absorb change. With that view, they can prioritize, stop or delay lower-value initiatives, and sequence the rest to avoid overload. This is often the most valuable and most neglected change management action, because it requires executives to make explicit trade-offs among their own priorities.

Prevention also depends on how change is designed and led. Involving the people affected in designing change improves solutions and builds ownership. Clear, consistent explanations of why change is needed, and honest acknowledgment of what will be difficult, build credibility. Adequate training, time and resources make adoption feasible. Equipping managers, who translate change for their teams, is especially important. Finally, finishing initiatives and celebrating real results rebuilds trust that change is worth the effort.

sections.heading: Recovering when fatigue has set in
paragraphs: When change fatigue is already present, adding more communication rarely helps. The first step is acknowledging the problem openly. Leaders who recognize that the organization has been asked to absorb too much, and who explain what they will do differently, can begin to rebuild trust. Concrete actions matter more than words: pausing or cancelling some initiatives, reducing reporting burdens, or giving teams more control over implementation timelines all signal that leaders are listening.

Recovery also involves restoring capacity. This may mean addressing staffing gaps, protecting time for learning, or simplifying processes that consume energy without adding value. It may mean reinvesting in manager support and in practices that strengthen psychological safety, so that people feel able to say when they are overloaded. Over time, completing a smaller number of well-supported initiatives successfully is the most effective way to rebuild an organization's appetite and ability for change.

sections.heading: How Datalidity helps organizations prevent change fatigue
paragraphs: Datalidity treats change capacity as something that can be measured and designed for. Using our Listen, Measure, Design, Deliver, Sustain methodology, we listen to employees and managers about their experience of change, measure change load and readiness across teams, and map the full portfolio of initiatives to reveal where pressure is concentrated. That evidence gives leaders a realistic basis for prioritization and sequencing. It also helps executive teams have a productive conversation about trade-offs, grounded in data about their own organization rather than in competing claims about which initiative matters most.

We then design change approaches with the people affected, equip managers to lead their teams through transition, and support delivery with practical change management. Ongoing pulse measurement and governance routines help leaders sustain a healthy pace. The aim is an organization that can change when it needs to, because its people have the capacity, trust and support to make change stick, rather than one that cycles through initiatives that never take hold.

faqs.q: What is the difference between change fatigue and resistance to change?
faqs.a: Resistance to change is usually an active response to a specific change, often rooted in concerns about its rationale, fairness or consequences. Change fatigue is a more passive, cumulative state of exhaustion and resignation caused by too much change over time. Resistant employees may argue against an initiative; fatigued employees may simply disengage. The two can coexist, but fatigue requires reducing load and rebuilding capacity, not only persuasion.

faqs.q: How do you measure change fatigue?
faqs.a: Change fatigue can be measured through pulse surveys that ask about workload, capacity, confidence in leadership and perceived volume of change, combined with operational indicators such as adoption rates, participation, absence and turnover in affected teams. Mapping which initiatives affect which groups, and when, shows where load is concentrated. Interviews and focus groups provide essential context, since people often express fatigue more candidly in conversation than in surveys.

faqs.q: What role do managers play in preventing change fatigue?
faqs.a: Managers are central. They translate organizational change into daily reality for their teams, answer questions, adjust workloads and notice early signs of strain. When managers understand the rationale for change, have the time and tools to support people, and can escalate concerns about overload, teams cope far better. When managers are themselves overloaded or excluded from planning, fatigue spreads quickly through the teams they lead.

insights.title: Equity-Centered Design
insights.meta_title: Equity-Centered Design: Principles, Methods and Practice
insights.meta_description: Equity-centered design explained: how it builds on human-centered design, its core principles, practical methods, and how organizations apply it responsibly.
insights.summary: How equity-centered design extends human-centered design to address power, history and systemic inequity, and what it takes to practice it with integrity.
insights.dek: Equity-centered design asks not only whether a solution works for its users, but who has power in the design process, whose needs have historically been ignored, and how a solution might reduce or reproduce inequity. It is a discipline of design and of accountability.
key_takeaways: Equity-centered design extends human-centered design by explicitly addressing power, history and the systemic causes of inequity.
It centers people most affected by a problem, especially those historically excluded, as partners and decision makers in design.
Designers examine their own positions and assumptions, recognizing that design choices are never neutral.
Practiced well, it produces solutions that work better for everyone, because designing for the margins strengthens the whole system.

sections.heading: What equity-centered design is
paragraphs: Equity-centered design is an approach to designing products, services, policies and systems that explicitly aims to reduce inequity and to avoid reproducing it. It builds on human-centered design, which places the needs of users at the center of the design process, but it adds a critical lens. It asks who defines the problem, whose voices shape the solution, who benefits and who bears the risks. It recognizes that systems often produce unequal outcomes not by accident but because of how they were designed, and that new designs can either interrupt or reinforce those patterns.

The approach has been developed by practitioners and organizations across education, public health, civic technology and community development. Groups such as Creative Reaction Lab, which articulated Equity-Centered Community Design, and the Stanford d.school's work on liberatory and equity-centered practices have shaped the field. While frameworks differ, they share commitments to examining power, honoring lived experience and building the capacity of affected communities to lead change. The approach is increasingly adopted by public agencies, foundations, healthcare systems and employers seeking to design more fairly and effectively.

sections.heading: How it differs from human-centered design
paragraphs: Human-centered design has been a powerful force for making solutions more usable and relevant. Its critics, however, note that it can treat users as research subjects rather than partners, that it often focuses on individual needs while overlooking structural causes, and that it rarely questions the power held by the designers and the institutions commissioning the work. A team can conduct excellent user research and still produce a solution that serves the majority well while failing, or harming, people at the margins.

Equity-centered design responds to these concerns in several ways. It asks designers to understand the history and context of the problem, including past harms that may shape trust. It shifts decision-making power toward the people most affected rather than simply consulting them. It examines how a solution might affect different groups differently and builds in safeguards. And it treats the design process itself as an opportunity to build capacity and leadership within communities, so that the benefits of the work extend beyond any single product or service.

sections.heading: Core principles
paragraphs: Several principles recur across equity-centered design frameworks. They begin with self-awareness: designers and sponsoring organizations examine their own identities, assumptions and positions of power, because these shape what they notice and what they ignore. They extend to the people most affected, who are engaged as co-designers and, where possible, decision makers. They require attention to history and systems, so that solutions address root causes rather than symptoms, and they emphasize accountability for outcomes over time.

These principles also have practical implications for how projects are scoped, funded and governed. They take time and resources, including compensation for community members who contribute expertise. They also require humility about what an external team can and should decide on behalf of others, and willingness to change course when communities identify concerns that the original brief did not anticipate. Leaders who commission equity-centered work should expect it to challenge some of their assumptions, and should plan for that from the outset.
bullets: Acknowledge and examine the designer's own power and assumptions.
Center people most affected, especially those historically excluded.
Understand history and context before defining the problem.
Share decision-making power, not just opportunities for feedback.
Assess differential impacts and design safeguards against harm.
Build lasting community capacity and remain accountable for outcomes.

sections.heading: Methods and practices
paragraphs: Equity-centered design uses many familiar design methods, adapted to its commitments. Research is conducted with attention to who is included and excluded, with recruitment that deliberately reaches people often missed, such as those with disabilities, limited English proficiency, unstable housing or irregular work schedules. Community members may be trained and paid as co-researchers. Journey maps and service blueprints are disaggregated to show how experiences differ across groups. Equity impact assessments examine how proposed changes would affect different populations before decisions are made.

Co-design sessions are structured to balance power: meeting in community settings, providing childcare and interpretation, compensating participants, and giving them real influence over choices. Prototypes are tested with those most likely to be harmed or excluded, not only with typical users. Measurement disaggregates outcomes by relevant characteristics so that improvements on average do not hide widening gaps. Throughout, teams document how community input shaped decisions, which is essential for maintaining trust and for demonstrating that participation was meaningful rather than symbolic.

sections.heading: Why it matters for organizations
paragraphs: Equity-centered design is sometimes seen as relevant only to public agencies and nonprofits, but its value is broader. Any organization whose customers, employees or communities are diverse risks designing systems that work well for some and poorly for others. A benefits enrollment process, a hiring system, a patient pathway or a financial product can all produce unequal outcomes if designed around an assumed typical user. These failures carry real costs, including lost customers, legal and reputational risk, and wasted talent.

Designing for those at the margins often improves outcomes for everyone, a pattern familiar from accessibility work, where features such as captions and curb cuts benefit far more people than those they were designed for. Equity-centered design also builds trust with communities and employees, which in turn improves participation, adoption and the quality of the information organizations receive. For leaders committed to fairness and to serving their full range of stakeholders, it offers a disciplined way to turn those commitments into concrete design decisions.

sections.heading: How Datalidity practices equity-centered design
paragraphs: Equity is central to how Datalidity works. Within our Listen, Measure, Design, Deliver, Sustain methodology, we listen first to the people most affected, recruiting deliberately to include those often left out and compensating community expertise. We measure outcomes disaggregated by relevant characteristics, so that gaps are visible rather than averaged away, and we use equity audits and analytics to identify where systems produce unequal results. That evidence helps leaders see which parts of a service or employee system are working for some groups and failing others, and where redesign will matter most.

We design with communities and employees as partners, sharing decision-making where possible, and we support delivery and governance that keep organizations accountable for equitable outcomes over time. Whether we are redesigning a public service, an employee experience or a community program, our aim is solutions that work better for the people who have been least well served, and therefore better for everyone who depends on them, including the organization itself.

faqs.q: What is the difference between equity-centered design and inclusive design?
faqs.a: Inclusive design focuses on making products and services usable by people with the widest possible range of abilities, circumstances and characteristics, often with a strong emphasis on accessibility. Equity-centered design shares that goal but adds explicit attention to power, history and systemic inequity. It asks who has decision-making authority in the design process, how past harms shape the problem, and whether a solution reduces or reinforces existing disparities in outcomes.

faqs.q: How do you involve communities in equity-centered design?
faqs.a: Meaningful involvement starts early, at problem definition rather than at the testing stage. It includes recruiting people most affected, meeting in accessible community settings, compensating participants for their time and expertise, providing interpretation and childcare where needed, and giving community members real influence over decisions. Organizations should explain how input shaped outcomes and maintain relationships beyond a single project, so participation builds trust and lasting capacity.

faqs.q: Can equity-centered design be used inside companies?
faqs.a: Yes. Companies use equity-centered design to improve hiring processes, performance and promotion systems, benefits, workplace policies, customer services and products. Internally, it means involving employees from underrepresented groups in designing systems that affect them, disaggregating data to reveal disparities, and assessing how changes will affect different groups. It helps organizations build fairer systems, reduce legal and reputational risk, and make better use of talent.

insights.title: Double Materiality
insights.meta_title: Double Materiality: Definition, CSRD Rules and Assessment
insights.meta_description: Double materiality explained: impact and financial materiality, how the EU CSRD applies them, how to run an assessment, and how it informs strategy.
insights.summary: What double materiality means, how it shapes sustainability reporting under the EU CSRD, and how to run an assessment that informs strategy, not just disclosure.
insights.dek: Double materiality asks two questions at once: how sustainability issues affect a company's finances, and how the company affects people and the environment. Now a regulatory requirement in Europe, it is reshaping how boards view risk and impact.
key_takeaways: Double materiality combines financial materiality, outside-in, with impact materiality, inside-out, to determine what a company must report.
The EU Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive makes double materiality the basis for sustainability reporting under European standards.
A credible assessment relies on evidence and engagement with affected stakeholders, not only internal judgment.
Used well, the assessment informs strategy, risk management and governance, not only compliance and disclosure.

sections.heading: What double materiality means
paragraphs: Materiality is the principle that determines which information is important enough to report. In financial reporting, information is material if it could reasonably influence the decisions of investors. Double materiality extends this idea to sustainability by adding a second perspective. A sustainability matter is material if it is financially material, meaning it affects or could affect the company's cash flows, performance, position, cost of capital or access to finance. It is also material if it is impact material, meaning the company's operations or value chain have actual or potential significant effects on people or the environment.

These two perspectives are often described as outside-in and inside-out. The outside-in view asks how the world affects the company, for example how climate change, labor shortages or regulation create risks and opportunities. The inside-out view asks how the company affects the world, for example through emissions, working conditions in its supply chain or the effects of its products on customers and communities. Under double materiality, a matter is reportable if it is material from either perspective, or from both.

sections.heading: Double materiality and the EU CSRD
paragraphs: The concept was articulated in European Commission guidance on non-financial reporting and has since been embedded in law through the Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive, known as the CSRD. The directive requires companies within its scope to report according to the European Sustainability Reporting Standards, developed by EFRAG, and makes a double materiality assessment the foundation of that reporting. Companies must determine which sustainability topics are material through both lenses, disclose their assessment process, and report on the impacts, risks and opportunities identified.

Scope, timing and some requirements of the CSRD have been subject to revision through European simplification initiatives, and companies should take current legal advice on their obligations. The underlying principle of double materiality, however, remains central to the European approach. This contrasts with frameworks focused primarily on investors, such as the standards issued by the International Sustainability Standards Board, which take a financial materiality perspective. The GRI Standards, by contrast, focus on impact materiality. Many multinational companies must navigate several of these frameworks at the same time.

sections.heading: How to conduct a double materiality assessment
paragraphs: A double materiality assessment begins by understanding the company's business model, operations and full value chain, upstream and downstream. Teams then compile a long list of potential sustainability matters, drawing on reporting standards, sector guidance, peer practice, regulatory developments and, crucially, engagement with affected stakeholders. For each matter, they assess impacts on people and the environment by considering severity, which includes scale, scope and irremediability, along with likelihood for potential impacts. Separately, they assess financial risks and opportunities by considering magnitude and likelihood over short, medium and long time horizons.

The results are combined to determine which matters are material and therefore in scope for reporting. Thresholds and methods must be documented, and the process should be reviewed and approved through appropriate governance, often including the audit committee or board. Because the CSRD requires assurance of sustainability information, the assessment must be robust, evidence-based and auditable, not a one-off workshop exercise. Companies should expect auditors to examine how stakeholders were engaged, how thresholds were set and how judgments were reached, so clear records matter as much as the conclusions themselves.
bullets: Map the business model and full value chain.
Identify potential impacts, risks and opportunities across sustainability topics.
Engage affected stakeholders and users of sustainability information.
Assess impact severity and likelihood on people and the environment.
Assess financial magnitude and likelihood across relevant time horizons.
Set thresholds, document judgments and obtain governance approval.

sections.heading: The role of stakeholder engagement
paragraphs: Impact materiality cannot be credibly assessed from inside the company alone. The people affected by a company's activities, including employees, workers in the value chain, local communities, customers and end users, often understand impacts that internal teams overlook. European standards expect companies to consider the views of affected stakeholders in their assessment, and well-designed engagement makes the result more accurate and defensible. Engagement also tends to strengthen relationships with the groups whose cooperation the company depends on, and it gives leaders an earlier view of issues that could later become legal, reputational or operational risks.

Effective engagement goes beyond surveys of senior internal stakeholders. It uses interviews, focus groups, community dialogue and representative organizations, such as trade unions or civil society groups, to understand experiences directly. It pays particular attention to vulnerable or marginalized groups, whose experiences of severe impacts may not surface through routine channels. It also draws on existing evidence, such as grievance mechanisms, employee listening programs and human rights due diligence, so the company builds on what it already knows rather than starting over each reporting cycle.

sections.heading: From compliance to strategy
paragraphs: Many companies approach double materiality as a reporting requirement, and for those in scope it is one. But the assessment also produces strategically valuable information. It maps where the company's most significant impacts lie and how sustainability issues could affect its financial resilience. That information can inform risk management, capital allocation, product strategy, supply chain decisions and workforce planning. It can reveal opportunities as well as risks, such as markets for more sustainable products or advantages from better workforce practices.

The connection between impact and financial materiality is often dynamic. An impact on workers or communities that is not financially material today can become so as regulation, litigation, consumer expectations or labor markets change. Companies that understand their impacts early can act before they become financial risks. Integrating the assessment into strategy and governance, rather than treating it as a separate reporting process, ensures that what the company discloses reflects what it actually manages.

sections.heading: How Datalidity supports double materiality assessments
paragraphs: Datalidity helps companies and investors conduct double materiality assessments that are rigorous, stakeholder-informed and useful for strategy. Within our Listen, Measure, Design, Deliver, Sustain methodology, we engage affected stakeholders directly, including employees, value chain workers and communities, and we draw on people analytics and existing data to measure the severity and likelihood of social impacts with evidence rather than assumption. Where data is missing, we design practical ways to collect it, so that each reporting cycle rests on a stronger evidence base than the last.

Our particular strength is the social dimension, including workforce, community and customer impacts, where engagement and analytics matter most. We help clients design assessment methods, governance and documentation that support assurance, and we connect the results to strategy, impact measurement and dashboards so that material issues are managed, not only reported. The outcome is reporting that is defensible and a management agenda that reflects the company's real effects on people.

faqs.q: What is the difference between single and double materiality?
faqs.a: Single materiality, often called financial materiality, considers only how sustainability matters affect a company's financial performance and value, which is the main concern of investors. Double materiality adds impact materiality, which considers how the company's activities affect people and the environment, regardless of whether those effects are currently financially significant. Under double materiality, a topic is reportable if it is material from either perspective.

faqs.q: Who needs to conduct a double materiality assessment?
faqs.a: Companies within the scope of the EU Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive must conduct a double materiality assessment as the basis for reporting under the European Sustainability Reporting Standards. Scope and timing have been subject to revision, so companies should confirm their obligations with legal advisors. Other organizations, including companies outside the EU with European operations and those preparing for investor or customer expectations, increasingly adopt the approach voluntarily.

faqs.q: How often should a double materiality assessment be updated?
faqs.a: Companies should review their assessment each reporting period to confirm it remains valid, and update it more fully when there are significant changes in the business, value chain, operating context or stakeholder expectations, such as acquisitions, new markets or regulatory developments. Many conduct a comprehensive assessment periodically and lighter annual refreshes, using ongoing stakeholder engagement and monitoring data to identify emerging issues between full cycles.

insights.title: Impact Measurement & Management (IMM)
insights.meta_title: Impact Measurement and Management (IMM): A Practical Guide
insights.meta_description: Impact measurement and management (IMM) explained: the five dimensions of impact, core frameworks, how to build an IMM system, and how to use data to decide.
insights.summary: A guide to impact measurement and management: the five dimensions of impact, the main frameworks, and how to build a system that improves decisions, not just reports.
insights.dek: Impact measurement and management is the practice of identifying, measuring and acting on the effects an organization or investment has on people and the planet. The emphasis on management is deliberate: the goal is not to count impact but to improve it.
key_takeaways: IMM is the ongoing practice of measuring effects on people and the planet and using that evidence to improve decisions.
The Impact Management Project's five dimensions, what, who, how much, contribution and risk, provide a widely used shared language.
Frameworks such as IRIS+ and the Operating Principles for Impact Management support consistent metrics and practice.
Effective IMM integrates stakeholder voice, focuses on a few decision-relevant metrics, and links findings to governance and resources.

sections.heading: What impact measurement and management means
paragraphs: Impact measurement and management, commonly abbreviated as IMM, is the process by which organizations and investors identify the effects of their activities on people and the planet, measure those effects, and use the evidence to make better decisions. It is used by impact investors, foundations, nonprofits, social enterprises, development finance institutions and, increasingly, mainstream companies and asset managers. The term emphasizes management because measurement alone has limited value. Data that is collected for reports but never informs strategy, resource allocation or program design does little to improve outcomes for anyone.

IMM covers the full cycle of setting impact goals, defining indicators, collecting and analyzing data, interpreting results with stakeholders, and adjusting strategy and operations in response. It considers positive and negative effects, intended and unintended, and it applies across the life of an investment or program. A mature IMM system treats impact performance with the same discipline as financial performance: it sets targets, monitors progress, reports to governance bodies and holds leaders accountable for results.

sections.heading: The five dimensions of impact
paragraphs: A major step toward a shared language for impact came from the Impact Management Project, a multi-stakeholder forum that convened practitioners to build consensus on how to describe and manage impact. Its work, now stewarded by Impact Frontiers, defined five dimensions of impact that together provide a complete picture of an outcome. Rather than asking simply whether impact occurred, the dimensions ask what outcome occurred, who experienced it, how significant it was, what the organization contributed, and how likely it is that impact differs from expectations.

These dimensions help organizations avoid common errors, such as reporting large numbers of people reached without considering depth of change, or claiming outcomes that would have occurred anyway. They also allow investors to compare and construct portfolios by the type of impact each investment contributes. Because they are descriptive rather than prescriptive, the five dimensions work alongside other frameworks and metrics. Many investors use them during due diligence to set expectations, during the holding period to monitor performance, and at exit to assess what impact was achieved and whether it is likely to endure.
bullets: What: the outcome and whether it is positive or negative for people or planet.
Who: the stakeholders experiencing the outcome and how underserved they are.
How much: the scale, depth and duration of the outcome.
Contribution: the difference made compared with what would have happened anyway.
Risk: the likelihood that impact differs from what was expected.

sections.heading: Frameworks and standards
paragraphs: Several frameworks support IMM practice. IRIS+, managed by the Global Impact Investing Network, provides a catalog of standardized metrics and core metric sets organized by impact theme, helping organizations select credible indicators and compare results. The Operating Principles for Impact Management, launched with the International Finance Corporation, set out a framework for integrating impact considerations across the investment lifecycle, from strategy and origination through monitoring and exit, with independent verification. The Sustainable Development Goals often provide a high-level reference for aligning impact objectives.

Other tools address specific needs. A theory of change articulates how activities are expected to lead to outcomes. Social return on investment values outcomes in monetary terms. Double materiality assessments, required in some jurisdictions, identify the most significant impacts for reporting. These frameworks are complementary rather than competing. The practical challenge is to choose a coherent combination that fits the organization's strategy and capacity, rather than adopting every framework and drowning in metrics.

sections.heading: Building an effective IMM system
paragraphs: An effective IMM system starts with clear impact objectives, grounded in a theory of change that explains how the organization's activities are expected to create outcomes. From there, organizations select a focused set of indicators, prioritizing those that inform real decisions. A small number of well-chosen outcome indicators, complemented by output and process measures, is more useful than a long list of metrics that no one has time to analyze. Data collection should be proportionate, integrated with operational systems where possible, and designed to minimize burden on participants and partners.

Analysis and interpretation are where measurement becomes management. Results should be reviewed regularly by people with authority to act, compared against targets and expectations, and discussed with stakeholders who can explain what the numbers mean. Findings should flow into decisions about strategy, budgets, program design, investment selection and engagement with portfolio companies, and the system itself should be reviewed and improved periodically as needs change. When results fall short, a good system helps teams diagnose whether the problem lies in delivery, in the underlying theory of change or in the data itself.
bullets: Define impact objectives anchored in a theory of change.
Select a focused set of decision-relevant indicators.
Collect proportionate data, including direct stakeholder feedback.
Review results regularly with decision makers and stakeholders.
Link findings to resources, incentives and governance.
Report transparently on both progress and shortfalls.

sections.heading: Centering stakeholder voice
paragraphs: The people experiencing outcomes are often the best judges of whether those outcomes are meaningful. Yet many IMM systems rely heavily on administrative data and organizational self-assessment, with little direct input from the people affected. Approaches such as lean data, popularized by the impact investor Acumen, and constituent feedback practices show that it is possible to gather timely, affordable and decision-relevant feedback directly from customers, beneficiaries, employees and communities. Short, well-designed surveys delivered by phone or text can reach people who would never attend a focus group.

Centering stakeholder voice improves IMM in several ways. It surfaces outcomes, including negative ones, that internal metrics miss. It helps organizations understand why results occur, not just whether they occur. It enables disaggregation, revealing which groups benefit most and which are left behind. And it reflects a principle of accountability: those whose lives an organization seeks to improve should have a say in how improvement is defined and judged. For investors, stakeholder feedback from portfolio companies can provide early signals of impact and business risk.

sections.heading: How Datalidity builds impact measurement and management systems
paragraphs: Datalidity designs IMM systems that are rigorous, proportionate and useful. Our Listen, Measure, Design, Deliver, Sustain methodology mirrors the IMM cycle: we listen to stakeholders to understand what outcomes matter, measure baselines and progress with credible methods, design indicators and processes that fit the organization, deliver implementation and capability building, and sustain the system through dashboards, governance and periodic review. We keep systems proportionate to each organization's size and capacity, so that measurement supports the work rather than consuming the resources meant for it.

We work with impact investors, private equity sponsors, foundations, nonprofits, public agencies and companies, often focusing on the social dimension of impact, including workforce, community and customer outcomes. We draw on the five dimensions of impact, IRIS+ metrics and theory of change to build coherent systems, and we help leaders connect impact evidence to strategic and investment decisions so that measurement leads to better outcomes for people, not only better reports.

faqs.q: What are the five dimensions of impact?
faqs.a: The five dimensions, developed through the Impact Management Project, are what, who, how much, contribution and risk. What describes the outcome and whether it is positive or negative. Who describes the stakeholders experiencing it. How much covers scale, depth and duration. Contribution considers what difference the organization made compared with what would have happened anyway. Risk assesses the likelihood that impact differs from expectations. Together they provide a structured, comparable description of impact.

faqs.q: What is the difference between impact measurement and impact management?
faqs.a: Impact measurement is the process of collecting and analyzing evidence about the effects of an organization or investment on people and the planet. Impact management is the use of that evidence to make decisions, set targets, allocate resources and improve outcomes. Measurement without management produces reports; management without measurement relies on assumption. The combined practice ensures that evidence about impact actually shapes strategy and operations.

faqs.q: How do impact investors measure impact?
faqs.a: Impact investors typically set impact objectives aligned with their strategy, assess expected impact during due diligence, often using the five dimensions of impact, and agree indicators with investees, frequently drawn from IRIS+. They monitor performance throughout the holding period, collect stakeholder feedback where possible, and assess impact at exit. Many align their practices with the Operating Principles for Impact Management and obtain independent verification of their impact management systems.
